# Results — Study 161 (Year-Ending-Five) on real Shiller S&P 500 data

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Source: Shiller S&P 500
monthly dataset (`_cache/shiller_sp500.parquet`), December-close prices used to compute
calendar-year log-returns.  Calendar years 1872–2025 (n = 154 annual returns; the
first usable return is 1872 = ln(Dec-1872 / Dec-1871)).  As-of **2026-06-15**.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | n years | Fingerprint (ret_pct col) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shiller S&P 500 monthly | 1872–2025 | 154 | `703f6b14e2eb` |

*n per last-digit bucket: ~15–16 (154 / 10 ≈ 15.4 per digit).  This is the structural
power floor — roughly 16 independent observations per last-digit hypothesis.*

## Full decennial cycle — mean calendar-year return by last digit

| Last digit | n | Mean % | Std % | Rank |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 | 15 | −0.34 | 16.61 | 10 |
| 1 | 15 | +4.03 | 19.19 | 8 |
| 2 | 16 | +2.39 | 13.41 | 9 |
| 3 | 16 | +4.78 | 20.02 | 7 |
| 4 | 16 | +6.24 | 18.04 | 5 |
| **5** | **16** | **+19.28** | **13.91** | **1** |
| 6 | 15 | +6.17 | 13.54 | 6 |
| 7 | 15 | −2.04 | 21.05 | 9 |
| 8 | 15 | +11.06 | 19.23 | 3 |
| 9 | 15 | +12.20 | 14.54 | 2 |
| Grand mean | 154 | +6.42 | 17.85 | — |

The pattern is stark: digit 5 averages **+19.28%** vs a grand mean of **+6.42%**.
Digit 0 ("the worst") averages **−0.34%**, dead last.  The two-digit folklore is
arithmetically correct in the Shiller sample.

## Digit-5 contrast and HAC inference

| Measure | Value |
|---|--:|
| Digit-5 mean | **+19.28%** |
| All-other-digits mean | +4.93% |
| Contrast (5 minus others) | **+14.35 pp** |
| Grand mean | +6.42% |
| HAC t-stat (Newey-West, fives vs grand mean) | **+3.21** |
| SE | 4.01% |
| n per bucket | ~16 |
| Low-power warning | YES — n=16 per digit is tiny |

The HAC t-stat clears the |t| ≥ 2 bar at **+3.21**.  However, n = 16 means a single
bad digit-5 year (like 1875's −3.7% or 2015's −0.0%) has a large influence.  Without
1935's +40.8% outlier the digit-5 mean falls from +19.28% to +17.84% — still the top
digit, but more modest.

## Permutation / multiple-comparisons correction

We are testing the best of 10 digits post-hoc.  The two permutation p-values:

| Test | p-value |
|---|--:|
| Digit-5 mean ≥ observed (+19.28%), single hypothesis | **0.00074** |
| Best-of-10 digit mean ≥ observed (+19.28%), corrected | **0.00806** |
| Multiple-comparisons inflation factor | **~10.9x** |

**Even the Bonferroni-by-simulation p = 0.008 clears a 5% threshold**, suggesting the
digit-5 outperformance is not merely "the best of 10 random draws."  However:

1. We are pre-selecting a specific hypothesis (digit 5 being THE best) *because*
   someone showed us the data first — the claim did not pre-register.
2. n = 16 per digit means any single influential decade can shift the conclusion.
3. The inflation factor of ~11x (close to the naive ×10 Bonferroni factor) confirms
   we are paying the full multiple-comparisons price, not a discounted one.

## Pre/post 1945 split (informal out-of-sample check)

| Period | n (digit-5) | Digit-5 mean | Others mean | Contrast |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Pre-1945 (1872–1944) | 7 | +17.8% | +1.0% | +16.8 pp |
| Post-1945 (1945–2025) | 9 | +20.4% | +8.1% | +12.3 pp |

The contrast holds in both sub-periods (pre: +16.8 pp; post: +12.3 pp), providing
informal support that this is not purely a pre-war artifact.  But n = 7 and n = 9 in
each half make any within-period inference essentially powerless.

## Individual year-5 returns

| Year | Return | Year | Return |
|---|--:|---|--:|
| 1875 | −3.7% | 1955 | +29.7% |
| 1885 | +19.8% | 1965 | +9.3% |
| 1895 | +0.5% | 1975 | +32.2% |
| 1905 | +15.6% | 1985 | +26.0% |
| 1915 | +29.0% | 1995 | +35.0% |
| 1925 | +22.6% | 2005 | +5.2% |
| 1935 | +40.8% | 2015 | −0.0% |
| 1945 | +32.3% | 2025 | +14.0% |

Three of 16 years ended flat or negative (1875, 1895, 2015).  Thirteen of 16 were
meaningfully positive.  The pattern is real in the sample, but the key question is
whether there is a *mechanism* or it is long-run noise (see references.md).

## Could you trade it? Decennial timing strategy

Holding S&P 500 except in digit-0 years (the "worst" bucket, go to cash):

| Strategy | Annualised return |
|---|--:|
| Buy-and-hold (all years) | +4.84%/yr |
| Avoid digit-0 years only | +5.01%/yr |
| Annual advantage | **+0.17%/yr** |

The annual timing advantage of correctly avoiding digit-0 years over 154 years is
**+0.17%/yr** — economically trivial.  A long-only investor who is already in the
market loses almost nothing by *not* timing around the decennial digit.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** HAC t = +3.21 on digit-5 vs grand mean; best-of-10
  permutation p = 0.008.  The digit-5 pattern clears the arithmetic bar, but
  n = 16 per bucket and the post-hoc nature of the claim cap it at WEAK.  There
  is no structural mechanism connecting the last digit of the year to equity returns.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** The timing advantage from the decennial cycle is
  ~+0.17%/yr — below any realistic estimation error or transaction cost.  A
  buy-and-hold investor beats the timer in any decade with above-average digit-0 or
  below-average digit-5 performance.
- **Myth-check: PARTIALLY REAL.** The folklore that "5s are the best, 0s are the
  worst" is arithmetically correct in the Shiller sample.  But "arithmetic truth in
  a 16-observation bucket is not a mechanism" — and that is the point.
